utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. Before I take the appearances, I note that we reconvene today under Rule 15 bis; Judge Harhoff being absent. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner (briefly), Matthew Olmsted, assisted by Ms. Susanti, replacing Mr. Smith again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mr. Mico Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Jessica Lacey, and Paula Lynch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Jason Antley appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- on the -- there's a brief ruling which the Chamber has. That is, on the 23rd of November, the Prosecution filed confidentially its 18th motion, providing notification of protective measures applying to Witnesses 223, 238, 240, and 248. The Trial Chamber affirms that in accordance with Rule 78(F)(i) the protective measures previously granted continue to have effect mutatis mutandis in the current proceedings and assign new pseudonyms to these witnesses as requested. Secondly, the -- there are two motions which have been filed in respect of which the Chamber is requesting expedited responses; that is, the Defence motion of the 29th of November to re-call Witness 191, in respect of which we would request the Prosecution to respond, orally would suffice, by Thursday of this week. And the second matter is the Prosecution's motion of the 23rd of November to reconsider the oral ruling to admit unsigned statements, and as regards this, we would request the Defence to respond by Friday of this week. Yes, Ms. Korner, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, first of all, in fact I was going to offer to respond orally to the request to re-call Witness 191 if there's time today. We've actually considered it, and we have a response. So not to delay the witness any further, but if there's time at the end of the day, we can deal with that fairly quickly and shortly, orally. Your Honour, I was also going to raise the request for reconsideration, also to invite Your Honours that there should be an expedited response, because, Your Honours, of course, there's a suggestion there that there should be a further witness called and/or the testimony of one of the witnesses should be expanded to deal with that, if Your Honours don't reconsider the ruling or don't rule in our favour. And so obviously that's a matter that is quite important that we get a ruling on. Your Honours, can I deal with a couple of other administrative matters, briefly. First of all, yesterday's witness, as Your Honours may have heard, he was taken into hospital and operated on. It is possible, our latest information last night from the Victims and Witness Unit was that there may have to be a further operation. He is going to be seen this morning, we hope, to ascertain what the medical prognosis is and whether or not he will be fit to give evidence. We would still hope at the end of the week, but if not, when. And whether he would be fit before the -- the break. So that's the latest position as we understand it. Your Honours, could we ask, if we may, please, for a ruling as soon as possible on our application to call a number of witnesses as -- under the provisions of 92 quater. Because, obviously, if Your Honours refuse the application, we would need to look for other witnesses, if they're available, to cover these adjudicated facts for which they have been filed. Your Honours, I raised last week the question of the 92 bis witnesses, and whether Your Honours would think it appropriate to read into the record a summary which is an expanded version of the 92 -- I'm sorry, the 65 ter summaries which accompany all of these so that there is a public record, at least for the witnesses who are not those who have protective measures, of what the witnesses say in those statements. The reason that we ask for a ruling as soon as possible is that obviously the summaries would have to be done, and we anticipate that we would perhaps deal with them at the beginning of the week of the 13th of December, if Your Honours feel this is an appropriate way of dealing with their evidence. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may respond to that, Ms. Korner, the -- when you would have raised it, I made inquiries and my -- what I have learnt so far is that this would be entirely novel in terms of 92 bis witnesses, so it may very well be that you would have to give further reasons for the -- this application before the Chamber is to definitively rule on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, my understanding is, in fact, the opposite, that it's been done in a number of cases. But, however, I rather took that for granted without making further inquiries as to the exact cases. So I will deal with that. And, again, I can deal with that at the end of the day, if there's time. Your Honours, we -- Your Honours agreed -- acceded to the Defence application to re-call, I believe it's Witness 181, I think it was. And we said we might have to apply for witness summons. He's been contacted. He doesn't require a witness summons. And he will be appearing -- he'd asked for a letter simply confirming that he's required to attend, which has been dispatched, or was going to be dispatched, this morning. And he will attend to be further cross-examined on January the 10th. He will be the first witness that -- that we call. Your Honours, finally - and I'm sorry to have to deal with this - Your Honours last week agreed, on Friday, that we could add Witness 161 -- I'm sorry, 261 to our witness list and order that he be called before the Christmas adjournment. Your Honours may recall that this been the subject of some controversy, this witness. When the Defence responded to our application to call him, they suggested that this was a Defence witness, that the witness had not said what was contained in the investigator's notes of the conversation with him; it was only notes, as opposed to a recorded interview. And, indeed, enclosed with their motion a statement from the Defence investigator which purported to support their assertions. Your Honours having ruled that 261 could be added to the Prosecution witness list on Friday, he was contacted on the Friday and told this and was asked if he was prepared to meet with the investigator and a lawyer in order that a proper interview could be conducted. As I say, all we have at the moment are investigator's notes. He agreed but said he would like a witness summons -- a Prosecutor's summons, which is what many of these witnesses have been given, and so arrangements were then going to be made this week. However, he was contacted again yesterday, and he spoke to both the investigator and the lawyer, and he -- he said that -- he was told that the summons that he was going to be received would be signed by the Prosecutor, and that he then said that he wanted a summons from the Court. He was asked -- well, perhaps I should just read the brief note I've been given of this. He said that he felt under pressure. And when he was asked to explain, he said he wasn't being pressured by anyone but he just felt stress from the situation. He complained that he -- that it had been misrepresented to him when he was seen in August that he was not going to be called as a witness, and he agreed that in fact that had been -- it had been explained to him that the decision had not yet been made. He was then asked whether the Defence had contacted him in the last two days, and he said that they had. He was asked directly whether it was an attorney for the Defence who had contacted him, and he said that he -- we had better speak to the Defence about this, as he wasn't sure whether he was allowed to divulge this information to us. And at the end of the consideration, he stated that he would only meet with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor if the Trial Chamber issued a mandatory Court summons. And those were his exact words, which were somewhat surprising words, if they were his own words and not someone else's. I inquired of both Defence counsel yesterday whether any of them had either personally or through investigators been in contact with the witness. I did not receive a reply yesterday. I was told this morning that it does appear that the investigator for the Zupljanin team did get in contact with him. I have no idea, because I've not been told, what was said by that investigator. But there are two matters. The first is that from Friday morning onwards when Your Honours issued the ruling this was a Prosecution witness on our 65 ter list. And as Your Honours know, because we've been through this over and over again, the Defence, of course, may contact witnesses but they must inform us that they intend so to do. No such notification was given to us. The second matter is this: In the light of this conversation and everything that has transpired from the motion, the response to the motion in other words, the Prosecution will no longer be calling Witness 161 [sic]. So that's the situation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you for the update, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I said "161"; it should be "261."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may be it's a matter for Your Honours that you might like to make an inquiry as to why there was this contact which without notification, which is, again, a breach of the -- the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can only assure Your Honours that I don't believe, after receiving this information from Ms. Korner, that I asked my investigator to prepare a statement to that effect, if any contact were made with this witness. So as soon as I get this confirmation, I will pass it on to the Prosecutors. Therefore, I'm not in a position at this moment to respond to what has been said here. What has been said by the witness is something that corresponds to what has been said, that is, that he doesn't want to be the Prosecution witness. And his official statement will be forwarded to Ms. Korner and to the Chamber if necessary. We opposed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krgovic please slow down. This is impossible to interpret. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm in a position to say that the Defence prefers to cross-examine the witnesses who have valuable information rather than to have them as Defence witness. So our intention and we think it is advantageous, to have witnesses testifying here as Prosecution witnesses and we only do the cross-examine. So our position is that we didn't in any way try to influence this witness to the effect that he should reject the summons received from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say, I'm not quite clear. I understood from what was said to me earlier that there had been contact between Mr. Krgovic's investigator and this witness, whereas the translation at page 7, line 6, reads, "if any contacts were made." So I'm not clear whether Mr. Krgovic is saying that there was a contact but he doesn't know the detail, or he says he doesn't even know now whether there was a contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not aware of any contacts. I have no such information. I have three investigators, and last night I sent them an official request to explain what happened and under which circumstances. As soon as I get this information, I will convey it to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So there we have it for the time being. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, those are the matters that I wished to raise. As I say, if there's sufficient time at the end of the session, I'll deal with the application to re-call the other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I now withdraw. Mr. Olmsted is taking the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. Because of the extant order in respect of the next witness, could the blinds be lowered so the witness can be escorted to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, since the next witness is a 92 ter witness, if you allow me, I'd like to give a brief -- a summary of his evidence for the record while he comes in. This witness describes how members of the Serb police, military, and paramilitary units attacked his village Gornja Bioca in Ilijas municipality in May 1992. The Muslim villagers thereafter took shelter in the woods where they remained for several days without food and water and then eventually surrendered to the Serb forces. They were then detained at the local school in Gornja Bioca for several days and interrogated by police officers. The witness and another detainee were then transported to Ilijas SJB where they were beaten and then detained for overnight. The next day, the witness was taken to the railway station in Podlugovi where he was placed in a basement with approximately 80 other non-Serb detainees. He'll -- he describes in his statements the conditions in that basement and also describes an incident where two gas cannisters were thrown into the basement and at least one detainee ultimately died from this gassing incident. After spending several days in the basement, the witness was taken to another detention facility, this time the Iskra warehouse in Podlugovi, where he was detained for approximately 70 days, along with over 100 other non-Serb detainees. He will likewise describe -- or he does describe in his statement the conditions ata that detention facility. Finally, in mid-August, 1992, the witness and the other detainees at the warehouse were transported to Planjo's House in Vogosca where they were forced to cut wood, dig trenches, carry ammunition, and act as human shields for the Bosnian Serb army. On the 1st of October, 1992, the witnesses managed to escape while he was assigned to digging trenches up at Zuc hill in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I gather that you are hearing me in a language that you understand, because of your responses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first of all, we welcome you to the Tribunal and thank you for your assisting by attending to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I would remind you that the solemn declaration that you have just made imposes upon you an obligation to speak the truth. And should you fail to do so, the Chamber is empowered to impose the penalties for perjury. The --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am going to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Now, the -- you would have, by virtue of orders previously made by this Tribunal, which we confirm, been granted the opportunity, for good and sufficient reason, to have your image distorted so that whereas members of the public who have a right ordinarily to know what is being said before the Tribunal would hear what you are saying but that they would be unable to identify you. Also, you have been granted, as a part of these protective measures, a pseudonym, and the -- we will, in the course of your testimony, refer to you by that pseudonym. We intend no disrespect when we refer to you by that pseudonym or as "Mr. Witness" instead of your name. It is merely as a means to ensure that no error is made by inadvertently revealing your identity. So I would first invite the usher to hand to you the pseudonym sheet, which the Prosecution has. And if you're satisfied that it correctly states your name and date of birth, you will sign it and hand it back to her, please. The pseudonym sheet is admitted under seal and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01730, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you would have previously testified before this Tribunal, and therefore it is only necessary for me to remind you of the procedure; that is, that the side calling you begins - in this case, it's the Office of the Prosecutor. And when they're finished with their questions, the side opposite would have a right to cross-examine you, and then the calling side can re-examine. And the Chamber may, at that stage or indeed at any earlier stage, themselves, have questions of you. You have been called under an expedited procedure which means that the time that the Prosecution would spend with you would be 20 minutes and that the -- counsel for the Accused Stanisic has indicated that they would require about 30 minutes. And, as presently advised, counsel for the Accused Zupljanin, have -- have indicated that they will not have any questions of you. But that may very well change in the course of -- after your testimony is -- after your examination-in-chief is complete. Counsel, are those times that I have indicated correct? 20 minutes for the Prosecution; 30 minutes for the Stanisic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. I meant to do an oral application for a slight extension of that time. I sent this to, I think, your legal officers. This witness can provide evidence regarding a number of photographs, a map, and a couple documents that are not part of his 92 ter package. And we think that this information, this evidence, will be useful for this Trial Chamber in its consideration of events in Ilijas. This is the only witness the Prosecution intends to call with regard to Ilijas, and therefore we think it's important that we at least familiarise the Trial Chamber with some of the locations as well as some of the documentation that is relevant to this municipality. So we're asking for 40 minutes to examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In total?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted. The -- 40 minutes. And the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we would -- I would invite Mr. Olmsted to begin his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: First I want to ask you a few questions concerning your written statements that make up your 92 ter package. Prior to testifying today, did you have the opportunity to review your written statements from 11 November 1996, 22 June 1997, 1 May 2003, and 23 June 2010?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And having reviewed them, are you satisfied that the information contained in these four statements is accurate and correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes, they are accurate and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: With the limited time that I have with you, I do want to clarify a few matters, a handful of matters, that are contained within those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can have P1449 - this is tab 1 - on the screen, please. It's not on the screen yet. At least on the screen that I have in front of me. Your Honours, we appear to have some technical difficulties. And this will make it hard for me to show this witness documents, because I can't see them on my screen. So if we may pause at this moment until we sort this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, are you going to ask the witness about the ethnic composition of Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That is part of what I was going to be asking him about, but mainly I'm -- I wanted to focus on his village which is the subject of his evidence and his statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well ... I'm going to try to do this blindly. Your Honours, I'm going to skip this. And maybe, if they can sort this out, I'll bring it up at the end. I just wanted to familiarise the Trial Chamber with this village.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, in your prior statements you describe the attack on the village of Gornja Bioca towards the end of May 1992. Can you tell us, did the non-Serbs offer any resistance to this attack?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were there any non-Serb military formations in the village?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did the non-Serb population in Gornja Bioca have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Well, those were hunting rifles. And perhaps someone had purchased weapons from the Serbs who were selling them to the Muslims and then later on they would come to pick up these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you said "they came to pick up these weapons." Who was "they"?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Once they captured them, they seized these weapons because they virtually asked them to return the weapons to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you say "they," is this the Serb forces who engaged in the attack on the village?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Well, those were -- yes, the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you just briefly describe the level of destruction that was caused by the -- this attack on your village? The destruction to the non-Serb property.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Well, shelling started first, which was followed by gun-shots -- or, rather, shots from heavy artillery as well as from automatic weapons. This happened at 7.30 in the evening, when it started. And it stopped at midnight. They fired a flare which indicated the end of the attack. However, they resumed the attack at around 5.00 next morning, and the shelling went on throughout the day. I suppose those were mortar shells falling onto the woods where the Muslims had fled from their houses, although some people did remain in their homes. All of this lasted for two or three days so that on one occasion, I believe that was during the second night of the attack, a group of people headed for Visoko and at one point they came across a machine-gun nest from which fire was opened and resulted in the death of two Muslims. I believe that two of them were wounded. This group went back to the forest where we had been ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And let me stop you there, because a lot of this is contained in your statements. I just wanted to clarify: During the shelling, were non-Serb houses destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Well, the following day, when the attack started at 5.00 a.m., they went through the village and torching the houses. In the middle of the village, there is a primary school where Serbs live, and further on from the school is where Muslims lived. So they headed from the school up there, and my house was first Muslim house in line. My house was set on fire, as well as the house of Raif Sehic. And we saw some other houses burning up there on the hills. On that day, these people who attacked the village went to the hill where Uzeir Semovic [phoen] and his son lived. They were in a garage or a shed or whatever, I don't know what it was. He killed this man and his son. They opened fire. The bullets penetrated the walls of the garage and wounded a little girl. We were on the other side, on another hill, and we were able to observe what was going on from that vantage point around those houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your prior statements you mention that the first place you were detained in was the school in Gornja Bioca, where you and other non-Serb detainees were interrogated by two police officers over the course of two days. You also mentioned that the commander of Police Station Srednje, Mlado Maksimovic, came to the school to check on the interrogations. Can you tell us, where is Srednje? Is that in Ilijas municipality?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Srednje is part of the Ilijas municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, what was Mr. Maksimovic's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In your prior statements you mention that on 3 June 1992 you and Paco Durmic were taken to SJB Ilijas, the building in Ilijas, where you were beaten and detained over night. Can you tell us, what was the ethnicity of Mr. Durmic?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Durmic was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 3419.86 on the screen. And if we can zoom in and focus on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, this is a recent photograph, but do you recognise this town?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes, it's Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the usher to hand you the electronic pen and ask you to circle the SJB building in Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell us, how many storeys does this building have?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: There's a ground floor and two storeys above that. Three storeys in all. So the ground floor and two storeys above.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us on which floor you and Mr. Durmic were beaten?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: On the highest floor. Or the second, if you start counting from the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And on which floor was the jail cell, the jail cell that you were detained in?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: The jail cell was one storey below, that is, on the first floor, the way we usually count. Or if you count the ground floor, then it's the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mention in your prior statements that there were five other persons detained along with you and Mr. Durmic in that jail cell who had been captured in Ahatovici. Can you tell us, what were their ethnicities, these other five men?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Four of them were Muslims. And one was the father of Pero Vujovic, who said to us then that he had driven fast, he had been speeding, and that that's why they had locked him up with us. But to my mind he was there only to overhear the conversations among us. He was then released, but we stayed in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01731.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we next have on the screen 65 ter 3419.67.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, the next place you were taken to and detained was the railway station in Podlugovi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes. There's still the same photograph on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, and the same on mine. I think that they're trying to work out a technical issue. There we go. And we'll rotate it.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes, this is the railroad station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So this is the railway station in which you were detained.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes. I was detained in the basement of this railway station building.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in your prior statements you mention that Serb guards threw in two gas canisters into the basement, through a window. Do you see that window on this photograph? And, if so, can you circle it.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the window. It's here. But they didn't use petrol. They used some sort of poison. There were two rooms; I was in the first room. And in the second room where this window was is -- they threw something in the room through that window. And some people were shouting it was gas and others said that it was poison. I noticed the smoke, and when I inhaled it I fell down and I had the feeling as if I were burning. And then someone said, Let's push the window-frame out so we can -- we can leave. And somebody else said, No, don't do it, they will shoot at us. But we were able to do so after all, we came out and went to the platform of the railway station and there was a semi-circle of Serb soldiers who had stockings over their heads. There was one man without a stocking. I know him. Sasa Savic; he went to school with me. So I'm certain that he was among those people then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01732, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 3419.68 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, after being detained in the railway station basement for several days, you were next taken to the Iskra warehouse in Podlugovi where you were detained for approximately 70 days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken to the Iskra warehouse where I stayed 70 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what happened to the detainees who remained in the basement of the railway station? Did they survive?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: They did not survive. In 1996, after the end of the war, they were found at Radica Potok. It's by a village called Ljesevo. They were all taken there and killed there. And after the war, their bodies were found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you help identify some of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes. I was called to identify them, and I was able to identify some.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us is an aerial photograph. Again, this is a recent photograph, but can you locate and circle for us the warehouse that you were detained in for approximately 70 days.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: It's this warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you also circle -- I don't know if you can tell from this aerial photograph, but can you circle the railway station.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes, here it is. We were taken from here. This is the bus-stop, by the way. And then we were taken to this building. And here there was the old primary school at Podlugovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you place a number 1 at the warehouse and a number 2 at the railway station.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: There's number 1, the warehouse; and here's number 2, the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In your prior statements you mention that over 100 people were detained that facility. What were their ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: You mean at the railway station?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, at the warehouse. The people who were detained at the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Oh, the warehouse. They were Muslims and there were also Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was -- looking at this warehouse, was the whole warehouse used as the detention facility or only certain rooms of it?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: No, only two rooms were used. One was locked. There was some parcels there; I don't know what was inside. Possibly tools or maybe some kitchen appliances.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During your time at this warehouse, were you and the other detainees ever allowed outside to get exercise?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: No. Nobody went outside. Only on one occasion, when something had to be done outside, they would take a couple of workers out until they did what had to be done and then they would return them. Sometimes there would be a tanker truck to clean the toilet, because there was no water inside. So maybe once in a week there would be a tanker truck for that to be cleaned because it stank horribly. And that's where we spent the 70 days. Once in 24 hours there would be a van that brought half a loaf of bread each or -- and that was it. That's what we got. Possibly some prisoners were allowed to receive food from some acquaintances, but those were people who were on good relations with the local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were any of the detainees held at the warehouse involved in armed resistance against the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Well, no, nobody. Because there were no organisations present there. Nobody put up resistance. And I'm 100 per cent sure that there was no armed conflict between Muslims and Serbs. It's only that the Serbs attacked and shot, whereas the other side didn't return fire at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01733, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have on the screen 65 ter 2976. And if we may turn to page 2 of both the English and B/C/S. I guess page 3 of the English then, because we have different pages here. There we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a list for exchange of captured persons from Ilijas municipality issued by the Serbian municipality of Ilijas dated 25 June 1992. Sir, you had the opportunity to review this list yesterday during proofing. Were you able to recognise any of the persons on these lists? I'm just speaking generally.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: The exchange on the 20th of June, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No. I don't want to talk about any exchanges at this point in time. I just wanted to ask you, you reviewed this list of names during proofing yesterday. Were you able to recognise the persons on this list? Did you know them?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: I knew these people but they were not exchanged on the 20th of June. Some of them were exchanged on the 25th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that is more or less my next question. Did you see these individuals on this list at any of the detention facilities in Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes. I was able to see them at the primary school at Gornja Bioca and in the Iskra warehouse at Podlugovi. The same people were detained there with me, the ones I recognise on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Under number 83 we see the name Bakir Sehic. Can you tell us, very briefly, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: He arrived toward the end of June, I believe it happened, maybe on the 20th or thereabouts. A man arrived who introduced himself as Mico, and he said that he was a Vojvoda of Vojislav Seselj, that he had come to defend the people in Bosnia, and that he was waging war in the mountains, or something, and that we were lying about there, and according to him we were having a good time and being well-fed. He contacted the prisoner warden, whose name was Slavko, and told him to single out two people and he would be back in the evening to take them away. However, Bakir Sehic was there near the bars, and I don't know why he picked him specifically. He turned toward the prison warden and said, Prepare him for me immediately. And opened the door. Slavko opened the door, Mico entered. He took some sort of string out of his pocket and he said, In the name of the law I arrest you. He tied his hands and took him away. He was later found in the mass -- mass grave where the others from the railway station were also found.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you identify his body?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01734, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I just have one last document to show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, what we have in front of us is a bulletin for 18 September 1992 from the prison department of the Serbian municipality of Vogosca. Sir, in your prior statements you describe how on 18 September 1992 you and 49 other detainees from Planjo's House were used as human shields at the front line on Zuc hill. This prison bulletin lists four detainees who were killed and seven who were wounded on Zuc hill. Can you tell us, just generally, how these detainees were wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Well, on that morning -- or, rather, a driver came every morning; his name was Milosevic. He came to fetch workers to take them to Zuc. On that morning, he came driving a bus. We were ordered to line up in front of that house, that is, the prison. And that bus driver and the prison warden Vlaco went to the bus and whispered to each other and then they came back and stood in front of the bus and Vlaco said to one of the guards to pick 50 prisoners, to count them. That's what he did. And then we were ordered to board the bus, which took us to Zuc. A large pit was there which had been dug out. It was maybe two or two and a half metres deep and some seven, eight metres wide. And we were ordered to go into that pit. And some sort of officer then came and he said to one of the soldiers that each platoon was in charge of 21 prisoners. Then they counted 21. And among those 21 there was me. We were told to stand in front of one soldier each. First there was a man who -- who stood in front of us and removed the mines that were in front of their trenches. And we were ordered to walk in the direction of the trenches of the Bosnian Muslims. While we were walking, I saw some trenches and there was a man standing there holding a rifle and looking at us. This went on for about 20 or 30 seconds. He didn't shoot. Next to me there was Mirsad Sehic. He was to my right. I looked at him and he looked back at me. And we looked at that man and then we took cover behind a tree. And then the fire started from both sides, and we were in between where they were shooting. I was able to see people falling down hit by bullets. I saw Enver Cinara, who was right next to me. I saw Mirsad, who was wounded in the leg. There was Muhamed Rizvo; he was also killed nearby. And Nermin Skando, who was also killed nearby. This all happened during that first attack. And then later, a couple of minutes later - or, actually, I don't know how long it lasted - the firing -- the fire stopped. And one of the prisoners was ordered to go toward the trench --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Just to clarify now. So the persons on -- listed on this document were among the killed and wounded on that day who were being used as human shields; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were there other persons who were wounded or killed that are not on this list that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes. When we came to the prison, the prisoners were saying that 13 prisoners had been killed. But the terrain was such that I was unable to see everybody. I didn't see those who were killed on the other side. And I can only confirm that the -- that the people on this list I didn't see them getting killed personally, whereas I saw others getting wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me clarify. I know we're going a little bit over, but let me clarify something that's in the transcript here. These four persons that are listed as having been killed by the enemy, Skando, Rizvo, Selimovic, and it says here "Cinaga" - I think that's an incorrect spelling - did you personally see these four individuals killed?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: I saw Enver Cinara fall. I saw Nermin Skando fall. I saw Hamid Rizvo fall. I saw Mirsad Sehic get injured. I saw Ismet Hujic get injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. That's -- that answers my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for going a little bit over. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we actually started a little late, so it balances out. Mr. Olmsted, the map, which there was the technical problem with at the beginning, you said you would return to at the end, do you still intend to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, just very briefly. If I could do that after the break. I just wanted to show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- Your Honours where -- where the village was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we take the break and return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, just to conclude, I want to show you the map that we wanted to show you earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can have P1449 on the screen. And can we enlarge it and go towards the upper portion of it. Enlarge it a little bit more. A little bit more. All right. Scroll up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, we have see in front of us a map of the Sarajevo area which includes Ilijas municipality, which we see in the upper portion of this map. Can you - perhaps the usher can give you the pen again - and could you circle for us your village, Gornja Bioca.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this map designates the areas that are predominantly Muslim in green and those that are predominantly Serb in blue, and we can see from this map that it appears that your village is surrounded by Serb villages. Was that, in fact, the case back in 1991/1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you want me to tender this in as a separate exhibit, or will you remember where the village is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I suppose, Mr. Olmsted, that the map speaks for itself but...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, no, I overheard Your Honour. It is. It's actually an exhibit. It's P11 -- P1449. So it's already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I think you will be able to find it when you are reviewing the evidence in the end, so I wasn't planning on tendering his circling of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I suppose it wouldn't hurt, because we'll pull it up to search around with a magnifying glass to find this village. It's useful, so we could have it marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01735.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, I will have only two questions. And since we already have the map in front of us, I would like to ask you the following. The town of Ilijas was under Serbian control during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, it was surrounded by Muslims throughout the war; did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: No, it wasn't surrounded by Muslims. Ilijas was connected with Vogosca and with Pale. And they had access towards Serbia, Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And apart from the accesses, what about the other sides? It was surrounded by Muslim armed forces. Just tell me whether you know; yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: That it was -- could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Apart from the access that you talked about on the other three sides, it was surrounded by Muslim armed forces during the war; did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: I know there were lines towards Visoko and in other directions around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And did you know that during these combat operations around it was one of the -- one of those towns that was the most badly destroyed in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Were you there during the war?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: During the four years [as interpreted] that I was in captivity, I was there. And immediately after the war in 1996, I arrived to Ilijas, and the town wasn't destroyed at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was four months of detention, not four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the combat operations around Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have another Prosecution exhibit on. It's their 65 ter list and it's 2976. In the Serbian version, could we have the last page, please. Actually, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, a moment ago the Prosecutor showed you this list of people to be exchanged and you recognised some of the names. Do you remember that you answered the Prosecutor's questions in relation to this document? Do you remember seeing this list?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes, I looked at this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You can see that this list was compiled by the Crisis Staff of Ilijas municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you know that there was a Crisis Staff in Ilijas municipality at the time.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that there was a Crisis Staff in Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like us to look at the previous page, which shows the name or the title of the document. And could we zoom in on the title, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness, I hope that you can read this. It says that this is a list exchange of captured person from Ilijas municipality for persons captured in Breza and Visoko municipalities.

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: The first exchange was in June, and a group of people who were imprisoned in the primary school in Ilijas were exchanged in the area of Breza. And this group of people, who were in the old primary school in Podlugovi, we spent 70 days there. Then we were transferred to Svrake. And the exchange was on the 15th of October, after I escaped from prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is for you to confirm that Breza and Visoko municipalities were under Muslim control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So the Crisis Staff of Ilijas municipality arranged this exchange with the representatives of Breza and Visoko municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: The exchange in June, you mean? I was not familiar with that exchange because the people who were in the primary school in Ilijas, well, I was not with them. I was at a different prison. I could see from the hangar where we were located, I was able to see the road and the buses, when a group of people who were exchanged to Breza were being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question is very simple. I would just like to you confirm --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it seems to call for speculation. There's no foundation that this witness would have been privy to negotiations between the Crisis Staff in Ilijas and any authorities in Breza or Visoko, as he was - as he has already testified - in detention at the time, at least until October 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I suppose if the question is refined in terms of what he is aware of or what he would have gotten a first-hand report of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that wasn't my question. Mr. Olmsted anticipated my questions. And my question is a lot simpler.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Since you confirmed that Breza and Visoko municipalities were under Muslim control, this exchange was done for Serbs who had been captured in the -- that area?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were exchanged. I just know that buses went towards Breza. As for whether there was an actual exchange or not, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to confirm, since you weren't there. What I want to know is who these people would have been exchanged for. Do you agree with me that these might have been Serbs from those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ST-004
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know that the buses travelled along the road, and we were told that these people were being taken towards Breza. As for whether they were exchanged or released, I don't know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. If you don't know, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does the Zupljanin Defence have any questions of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't have a question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we thank you for your assistance. You are now released, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, are you forgetting something?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honours. At this time the Prosecution would move to admit the 92 ter package of this witness, which includes his four statements and two associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, a memorandum will be distributed to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm back to deal with the motion that Your Honours asked me to deal with. The Defence requested, yesterday, that Witness 191, ST-191, be re-called for further cross-examination on the basis of the disclosure of a document on the 17th of May of this year. The document was one, as Your Honours remarked in -- I think I'll just wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, I was just checking something. Your Honours, this was a document to which the Republic of Serbia had put in an ex parte objection to its use. In fact, in June of 2009 Prosecution had responded, on 18th June, 2009, opposing the redaction sought. It was redacted rather than an objection in whole. And, as I say, Your Honours made an oral decision on the 17th of May. Now, that was after Witness 191 had, in fact, completed his testimony. However, aside from the unbelievable gap, even by the standards of cases here, between the admission of that document, the testimony of the witness, and this application, Your Honours, one of the reasons asserted why he should be re-called is that another witness, ST-182, produced a document which related to the meeting of the Teslic political leadership with General Mladic, and the Defence asserts in paragraph 4 that ST-182 was not present at the meeting and therefore could not verify the accuracy or veracity of the contents of the documents based on any first-hand knowledge. That is, in fact, incorrect in this sense, or -- firstly, the witness told the Court that he obtained this information from a VRS officer who was present at the meeting; and, second, he said that he'd verified the information through other sources. And Your Honours will find that in the transcript at pages 10947 through to 10951. Your Honours have ordered the Prosecution to complete its evidence, bar the two witnesses that have been agreed to call in January, before December. It's unlikely that we can get him here before the close of the case. But in the end result, having corrected what we think is a slight misrepresentation of what the evidence was, we're going to leave it in the hands of Your Honours to decide whether the witness should be re-called for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we now have your response, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep. Your Honours, however, may I also mention, while I'm here and on my feet, the question of the Status Conference. I have had communication with the Defence for Stanisic, and they are agreeable, I think -- they're agreed that the 13th of December would be suitable. We would almost certainly complete all the evidence we have for next week. I haven't received a response from the Zupljanin team. But, Your Honours, we think, for obvious reasons, that the sooner in the week the Status Conference can be held, the better. So we leave it -- obviously it's a matter for Your Honours, but we would suggest that's a suitable date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, the -- we thought, from the last communication that we had, in the terms of the flow of your witnesses, that there may have been a spillover into that week. So I suppose the 13th is a tentative fixture which may very well slide to later in the week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One of the witness we would have had next week is one ST-161 who we withdrew this morning. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I keep saying 161. 261. Thank you very much, Your Honour. So we think it improbable that it will go into the following week. But I agree; it's a tentative fixture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And is that it for the day? I know that it's a videolink scheduled for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. That's why we can't go any further today. That is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, anything on the 92 bis and the summaries to be read?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the moment, the person who gave me the information wasn't available. We've been doing some research, and, at the moment, Your Honours may well be right, and I may well have been given duff information, and I may have to withdraw the application. Although, Your Honour, even if not been done before, it is something we'd ask Your Honours to consider. It's a way, at least, of the public knowing what evidence is forming part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we'll see. Thank you very much. So we take the adjournment to 9.00 tomorrow morning, in this courtroom I believe we still are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of December, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.18 a.m.,
